rows.question: Does the technical documentation of a high-risk AI system require to provide specifications regarding the required hardware?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 11, a provider must draw up technical documentation containing the information set out in Annex IV, which expressly requires a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV point 1(e)) and, as part of the system's development description, the computational resources used to develop, train, test and validate it (Annex IV point 2(c)).
criteria_text: Yes
Description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV.1.e)
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'Yes' as the position, which matches the required verdict in criterion 1.
The answer explicitly provides the substance of the requirement by stating that Annex IV point 1(e) requires a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and coherent prose suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: I have a medical device that has an AI system as a safety component. The medical device is classified "medium-risk" and undergoes a 3rd party conformity assessment. Is the AI system "medium risk" too? If yes, why? If not, why not?
rows.answer: No. The EU AI Act does not recognise a "medium-risk" tier. Because the AI system is a safety component of a medical device listed in Annex I (Regulation (EU) 2017/745) and that device undergoes third-party conformity assessment, both conditions of Article 6(1)(a) and (b) are satisfied, so the AI system is classified as high-risk under the Act regardless of the device's sectoral risk class. Under Article 43(3), the provider must follow the MDR notified-body conformity assessment procedure, integrating the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements of the AI Act into that single procedure, resulting in one CE marking under Article 48.
criteria_text: Yes - high-risk (AI Act has no "medium-risk" category)
Condition (a): AI system is safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation (medical devices under Regulation (EU) 2017/745)
Condition (b): that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment
Both conditions cumulative under Article 6(1), irrespective of the device's own sectoral risk classification
criterion_remarks: The answer correctly states that the EU AI Act does not recognise a 'medium-risk' tier and concludes the AI system is high-risk, aligning with the Act's binary classification.
The answer explicitly states that the AI system is a safety component of a medical device covered by Annex I legislation (citing Regulation (EU) 2017/745), conveying the substance of condition (a).
The answer clearly states that the medical device undergoes third-party conformity assessment, satisfying condition (b).

The answer explains that both Article 6(1)(a) and (b) conditions are met and that the classification as high-risk applies regardless of the device's sectoral risk class, capturing the cumulative and overriding nature of Article 6(1).
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents actionable regulatory information coherently.

rows.question: We want to deploy an AI system that performs biometric verification solely to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be. Is this system prohibited? Is it high-risk?
rows.answer: Not prohibited. A biometric verification system whose sole purpose is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be is explicitly excluded from the Annex III(1)(a) high-risk listing for remote biometric identification systems. Because the system falls outside Annex III(1)(a) by that express carve-out, it is not high-risk under Article 6(2). It is also none of the eight prohibited practices in Article 5(1). Unless the system is a safety component of a product covered by the Annex I Union harmonisation legislation requiring third-party conformity assessment, which would engage Article 6(1), it is not high-risk. If the system interacts directly with natural persons, the provider must comply with the Article 50(1) transparency obligation to inform them they are interacting with an AI system.
criteria_text: No, not prohibited
No, not high-risk
Falls within Annex III.1(a) biometric verification exclusion
criterion_remarks: The answer states the system is not prohibited and correctly explains it is not one of the eight prohibited practices under Article 5(1).
The answer concludes the system is not high-risk, explaining it falls outside Annex III(1)(a) and does not meet Article 6(1) unless additional conditions are met, which are not indicated here.
The answer explicitly states the system falls within the Annex III.1(a) exclusion for biometric verification systems with the sole purpose of confirming identity.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Which article of the EU AI Act governs human oversight measures?
rows.answer: Article 14 governs human oversight for high-risk AI systems, requiring they be designed so natural persons can effectively oversee them during use. Article 14(4) specifies the operative measures: the oversight persons must be enabled to understand the system's capabilities and limitations (Article 14(4)(a)), remain aware of automation bias (Article 14(4)(b)), correctly interpret the system's output (Article 14(4)(c)), decide to disregard, override, or reverse the output (Article 14(4)(d)), and intervene or halt the system via a stop button or similar procedure (Article 14(4)(e)). Article 14(5) adds a two-person verification rule for remote biometric identification systems under Annex III(1)(a), waivable where Union or national law considers it disproportionate for law enforcement, migration, border control, or asylum purposes.
criteria_text: Article 14
Design for effective human oversight during use
Aim: prevent/minimise risks to health, safety, fundamental rights
Measures built in by provider and/or implemented by deployer
Overseers enabled to understand, monitor, interpret, override, and halt the system
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that Article 14 governs human oversight for high-risk AI systems.
The answer states that high-risk AI systems must be designed so natural persons can effectively oversee them during use, which captures the substance of design for effective human oversight.
By stating that oversight aims to prevent or minimise risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights, the answer reflects the purpose specified in Article 14(2), even if indirectly.

The answer refers to measures built in by the provider and those to be implemented by the deployer through reference to Article 14(3)(a) and (b), satisfying the criterion by stating their existence and origin.
The answer lists all five enabling capabilities under Article 14(4)(a)-(e), including understanding, monitoring, interpreting, overriding, and halting the system, thus fully covering the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents information in a logical, actionable manner.

rows.question: Under what conditions should providers of general-purpose AI models be subject to exceptions regarding transparency-related requirements, if any? And what do those exceptions not cover?
rows.answer: The exceptions to the GPAI transparency-related obligations are set out in Article 53(2). The Article 53(1)(a) duty to draw up and keep up-to-date the technical documentation of the model (Annex XI) and the Article 53(1)(b) duty to provide information and documentation to downstream providers (Annex XII) do not apply to providers that release the model under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution, where the model parameters, including the weights, and information on the model architecture and usage, are made publicly available. The exception does not cover the remaining Article 53(1) obligations: the policy to comply with Union copyright law (Article 53(1)(c)) and the publicly available, sufficiently detailed summary of the training content (Article 53(1)(d)) apply regardless of the licence. The exception also does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk (Article 53(2), second subparagraph), which remain subject to the full Article 53 obligations together with the Article 55 systemic-risk duties.
criteria_text: Yes, exceptions exist
Condition: model released under free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution
Condition: parameters (weights, architecture info, usage info) made publicly available
Exception covers only points (a) and (b) of Article 53(1), not (c)/(d)
Exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly acknowledges the existence of exceptions under Article 53(2).
The answer states the model must be released under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification, and distribution.
The answer specifies that parameters, including weights, architecture, and usage information, must be made publicly available.
The answer clearly limits the exception to points (a) and (b) of Article 53(1), and explicitly excludes (c) and (d) from the exception.
The answer states that the exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, which remain subject to full obligations.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents information in a logical, actionable manner for a compliance audience.

rows.question: What are the administrative fines for non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices?
rows.answer: Article 99(3) imposes administrative fines of up to EUR 35 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7% of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, for non-compliance with the prohibited AI practices listed in Article 5. This is the highest of the three fine ceilings in the Act's penalty regime. Under Article 99(6), for SMEs including start-ups, the applicable ceiling is the lower of the fixed amount or the turnover percentage.
criteria_text: EUR 35,000,000 or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher
Applies to non-compliance with Article 5 prohibited AI practices
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states the substance of the fine amount and the 'whichever is higher' rule, using slightly different formatting but preserving the meaning.
The candidate answer explicitly links the fines to non-compliance with the prohibited AI practices in Article 5, stating the substance required by the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral register; clearly structured prose with no self-reference, hedging, or informality; additional context about SMEs and penalty tiers does not detract from clarity or appropriateness.

rows.question: What is a deep fake according to the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: ‘deep fake’ means AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful;
criteria_text: AI-generated or manipulated content
Image, audio, or video
Resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events
Falsely appears authentic or truthful to a person
criterion_remarks: The answer states that deep fakes are AI-generated or manipulated content, which matches the substance of criterion 1.
The answer specifies image, audio or video content, which matches the substance of criterion 2.
The answer includes that the content resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events, which matches the substance of criterion 3.
The answer states the content would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful, which matches the substance of criterion 4.
rows.tone_remark: The response is concise, uses neutral and professional language consistent with regulatory definitions, and presents the information in a single, clear sentence suitable for a compliance context.

rows.question: What are all the risk categories in the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: The EU AI Act sets four risk tiers plus a separate regime for general-purpose AI models: unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5; and high-risk systems are classified under Article 6 (an Annex I product safety component, or an Annex III use case) and carry the Chapter III Section 2 obligations. Limited-risk systems carry the Article 50 transparency duties, minimal-risk systems avoid Chapter III high-risk requirements but retain Article 4 AI literacy duties, with voluntary codes under Article 95, and general-purpose AI models are governed separately under Articles 51 to 56, with added obligations under Article 55 for models classified as having systemic risk under Article 51.
criteria_text: Unacceptable risk - prohibited practices (Article 5)
High risk - Article 6, referencing Annex I (product safety) and Annex III (use cases)
Limited risk - transparency obligations (Article 50)
Minimal or no risk - no mandatory obligations, voluntary codes of conduct (Article 95)
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5, conveying the substance of the criterion.
The answer identifies high-risk systems under Article 6 and references both Annex I and Annex III, capturing the full substance of the criterion.
The answer states that limited-risk systems are subject to Article 50 transparency duties, which matches the substance of the criterion.
The answer acknowledges minimal or no risk systems are not subject to high-risk obligations and notes the availability of voluntary codes under Article 95, satisfying the substance of the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; presents information in a coherent, regulatory-appropriate manner without self-reference or informality.

rows.question: Can an operator that is not a provider according to the EU AI Act, for example a deployer, take actions on a given high-risk AI system such that it can be effectively seen as a provider by the authorities? If yes, what kind of action would result in such an outcome?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 25(1), a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is deemed to be the provider of a high-risk AI system, and takes on the provider obligations in Article 16, in any of three cases. First, if it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market (Article 25(1)(a)). Second, if it makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk (Article 25(1)(b)). Third, if it modifies the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk (Article 25(1)(c)). In each of these three cases the operator assumes the provider obligations in Article 16, and the initial provider is no longer considered the provider of that specific system under Article 25(2).
criteria_text: Yes
Putting own name/trademark on a high-risk AI system already on the market/in service (Article 25(1)(a))
Substantial modification to a high-risk AI system already on the market/in service that remains high-risk under Article 6 (Article 25(1)(b))
Modifying the intended purpose of a non-high-risk (incl. general-purpose) AI system such that it becomes high-risk under Article 6 (Article 25(1)(c))
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states 'Yes' as its first word, clearly affirming that a non-provider operator can be seen as a provider.
The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(a) by explaining that putting one's name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already on the market/in service triggers provider status.
The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(b) by describing substantial modification of a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk as a triggering action.

The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(c) by explaining that modifying the intended purpose of a non-high-risk AI system (including general-purpose) so that it becomes high-risk results in provider status.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and logical flow; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: According to Article 1, what is the objective of the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: Article 1(1) states that the Regulation's purpose is to improve the functioning of the internal market and promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI, while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety, and fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law, and environmental protection, against harmful effects of AI systems, and supporting innovation. Article 1(2) implements this objective by laying down harmonised rules on placing on the market, prohibitions, high-risk requirements, transparency rules, general-purpose AI model rules, governance and enforcement, and innovation-support measures.
criteria_text: Improve functioning of the internal market
Promote uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI
Ensure high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights (incl. democracy, rule of law, environment) against harmful effects of AI systems
Support innovation
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer explicitly states that the purpose includes improving the functioning of the internal market.
The candidate answer explicitly states the promotion of human-centric and trustworthy AI.
The candidate answer includes the full scope of protection—health, safety, fundamental rights, democracy, rule of law, and environmental protection—against harmful effects of AI systems.
The candidate answer explicitly mentions supporting innovation as part of the purpose.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured prose that clearly conveys regulatory content without self-reference or informality.

rows.question: Is an AI system used to structure or deduplicate information for a use case listed in Annex III considered high-risk?
rows.answer: No. Structuring or deduplicating information is a narrow procedural task, so the system falls under the Article 6(3) first subparagraph point (a) derogation and is not high-risk, provided it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and does not materially influence the outcome of decision making; the other limbs are (b) improving the result of a previously completed human activity, (c) detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, and (d) performing a preparatory task, and the derogation never applies where the system profiles natural persons. Under Article 6(4) a provider relying on the derogation must document the assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service, and register it under Article 49(2).
criteria_text: No
Falls under narrow procedural task derogation, Article 6(3), first subparagraph, point (a)
Exception: remains high-risk if system performs profiling of natural persons
Provider must document the assessment before placing on market/putting into service (Article 6(4))
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'No' as its first word and maintains that position throughout, clearly aligning with the required verdict.

The answer explicitly states that structuring or deduplicating information is a narrow procedural task and that it falls under Article 6(3), first subparagraph, point (a), capturing the substance of the criterion.

The answer includes the condition that the derogation does not apply if the system profiles natural persons, stating 'the derogation never applies where the system profiles natural persons', which conveys the required exception.

The answer references Article 6(4) and states that the provider must document the assessment before market placement or putting into service, satisfying the requirement to state the substance of the obligation.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and self-contained regulatory explanation without self-reference, hedging, or informality; well-structured and actionable.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what jurisdiction does the Court of Justice of the European Union have over Commission decisions fixing fines on providers of general-purpose AI models, and what can the Court do with the fine?
rows.answer: Article 101(5) grants the Court of Justice of the European Union unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions fixing fines on providers of general-purpose AI models under that Article. The Court may cancel, reduce, or increase the fine imposed. The fines subject to this review are those the Commission may impose under Article 101(1) for infringements of Chapter V obligations, failure to comply with information requests or measures, or supplying incorrect or misleading information, up to 3% of worldwide annual turnover or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher.
criteria_text: Unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions fixing a fine
Court may cancel the fine
Court may reduce the fine
Court may increase the fine
criterion_remarks: The answer states the Court has 'unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions fixing fines,' which conveys the substance of criterion 1.
The answer explicitly states the Court 'may cancel the fine,' matching the substance of criterion 2.
The answer includes that the Court 'may reduce the fine,' directly satisfying criterion 3.
The answer states the Court 'may increase the fine,' which matches the substance of criterion 4.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear, coherent structure and no self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: When registering a high-risk AI system in the EU database under the EU AI Act, what specific information must the provider submit? List the required items.
rows.answer: Annex VIII, Section A sets out the thirteen items a provider (or authorised representative) must enter into the EU database under Article 49(1) read with Article 71(2): the provider's name, address and contact details; the name, address and contact details of any person submitting on the provider's behalf; the authorised representative's name, address and contact details where applicable; the AI system trade name and any additional unambiguous reference allowing identification and traceability; a description of the intended purpose and of the components and functions supported; a basic and concise description of the information used by the system and its operating logic; the status of the AI system (on the market, in service, no longer placed on the market, or recalled); the type, number and expiry date of the conformity-assessment certificate; a scanned copy of that certificate; the Member States in which the system has been or is being placed on the market, put into service or made available; a copy of the EU declaration of conformity; electronic instructions for use; and an optional URL for additional information.
criteria_text: Contact details of the provider, of any person submitting on its behalf and of the authorised representative, where applicable (Annex VIII, Section A, points 1 to 3)
AI system trade name and an unambiguous reference allowing identification and traceability (point 4)
Intended purpose and the components and functions the system supports (point 5)
Basic and concise description of the data and inputs used and the operating logic (point 6)
Market status and the notified body certificate details with a scanned copy, where applicable (points 7 to 9)
Member States concerned, a copy of the EU declaration of conformity and the electronic instructions for use (points 10 to 12)
criterion_remarks: The answer includes the provider's contact details, those of any person submitting on its behalf, and the authorised representative where applicable.
The answer states the requirement for the AI system trade name and an unambiguous reference for identification and traceability.
The answer includes a description of the intended purpose and the components and functions supported by the system.
The answer provides a basic and concise description of the information used and the system's operating logic.
The answer specifies the system's status and includes the certificate type, number, expiry date, and a scanned copy where applicable.
The answer lists the Member States concerned, a copy of the EU declaration of conformity, and electronic instructions for use.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and complete sentences.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, when a high-risk AI system is found to conform with the requirements, what information must the Union technical documentation assessment certificate contain?
rows.answer: Under Annex VII point 4.6, where the notified body finds the high-risk AI system conforms with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, it issues a Union technical documentation assessment certificate. Per Annex VII point 4.6, that certificate must indicate the name and address of the provider, the conclusions of the examination, the conditions (if any) for its validity, and the data necessary for the identification of the AI system. Under Article 44(1) the certificate must be drawn up in a language which can be easily understood by the relevant authorities in the Member State in which the notified body is established, and under Article 44(2) it is valid for the period it indicates, which may not exceed five years for AI systems covered by Annex I and four years for AI systems covered by Annex III.
criteria_text: Language: drawn up in a language easily understood by the relevant authorities of the Member State where the notified body is established
Validity period stated: not exceeding five years (Annex I systems) or four years (Annex III systems)
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states that the certificate must be drawn up in a language easily understood by the relevant authorities in the Member State where the notified body is established, which matches the substance of criterion 1.
The candidate answer specifies that the validity period may not exceed five years for Annex I systems and four years for Annex III systems, conveying the substance of criterion 2.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and coherent prose suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: Under Article 10(5) of the EU AI Act, when may a provider of a high-risk AI system process special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction, and what key safeguards/conditions must be met?
rows.answer: Under Article 10(5), a provider of a high-risk AI system may exceptionally process special categories of personal data only to the extent strictly necessary to ensure bias detection and correction, subject to appropriate safeguards. These conditions apply in addition to, and not instead of, Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680. Article 10(5) requires all of the following: the bias work cannot be done with other data, including synthetic or anonymised data (a); technical limits on re-use plus state-of-the-art security and pseudonymisation (b); strict controls and documentation of access so that only authorised persons under appropriate confidentiality obligations can reach the data (c); the data are not transmitted, transferred or otherwise accessed by other parties (d); deletion once the bias is corrected or the retention period ends, whichever is first (e); and records of processing documenting why it was strictly necessary (f).
criteria_text: Only where strictly necessary for bias detection/correction under Art 10(2)(f)-(g), and cannot be effectively achieved with other data (incl. synthetic/anonymised)
Technical re-use limitations plus state-of-the-art security/privacy-preserving measures, including pseudonymisation
Strict, documented access controls limited to authorised persons under confidentiality obligations, with no transmission/transfer/access by other parties
Deletion once bias corrected or retention period ends, whichever is first
Processing records document necessity and why other data would not suffice
Additional to, not a substitute for, obligations under GDPR, EUDPR and the Law Enforcement Directive
criterion_remarks: The answer states that processing is allowed only when strictly necessary for bias detection/correction and cannot be effectively achieved with other data, including synthetic or anonymised data.
The answer includes technical limitations on re-use and specifies state-of-the-art security measures and pseudonymisation.
The answer describes strict, documented access controls limited to authorised persons under confidentiality obligations and explicitly prohibits transmission, transfer, or access by other parties.
The answer states that the data must be deleted once bias is corrected or the retention period ends, whichever comes first.
The answer mentions that records must document why processing was strictly necessary, satisfying the requirement to justify why other data would not suffice.
The answer clarifies that the conditions are in addition to, and not a substitute for, GDPR, EUDPR, and the Law Enforcement Directive.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and coherent prose suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must a provider of a high-risk AI system supply to the deployer in the instructions for use? List the required categories of information.
rows.answer: Article 13(3) governs the required content of instructions for use, which must include the provider's identity and contact details, the system's characteristics, capabilities and limitations covering its intended purpose, the level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity (including metrics) tested and validated under Article 15, any known or foreseeable circumstances that may pose risks to health, safety or fundamental rights under Article 9(2), where applicable the system's technical capabilities to explain its output, where appropriate its performance regarding specific persons or groups, where appropriate specifications for input data or information on training, validation and testing datasets, and where applicable information enabling deployers to interpret and appropriately use the system's output. Article 13(3) also requires the human oversight measures under Article 14, the system's expected lifetime, and necessary maintenance and care measures.
criteria_text: Provider and, where applicable, authorised representative identity/contact details

Characteristics, capabilities and performance limitations (intended purpose, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity levels, foreseeable risks, explainability capabilities, performance for specific groups, input data specifications)
Pre-determined changes to the system and its performance
Human oversight measures under Article 14
Computational/hardware resources needed, expected lifetime, and maintenance/care measures
Description of logging mechanisms under Article 12, where relevant
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that the instructions must include the provider's identity and contact details, satisfying the first criterion.

The answer covers all sub-elements of criterion 2: intended purpose, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity levels with metrics, foreseeable risks to health/safety/fundamental rights, explainability capabilities, performance for specific groups, and input data specifications or dataset information.
The answer does not mention pre-determined changes to the system and its performance, which are required under Article 13(3)(c).
The answer explicitly references human oversight measures under Article 14 as required by Article 13(3)(d).
While the answer mentions expected lifetime and maintenance measures, it omits computational and hardware resources needed, which is a required element under Article 13(3)(e).
The answer fails to mention the description of logging mechanisms under Article 12, which is required where relevant under Article 13(3)(f).
rows.tone_remark: The response uses professional, neutral, third-person language, is well-structured, and avoids self-reference or hedging. It clearly organizes the information in a manner suitable for regulatory compliance use.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) Article 95, who may draw up codes of conduct, and which bodies must encourage and facilitate their drawing up?
rows.answer: Under Article 95(1), the AI Office and the Member States shall encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct. Article 95(3) provides that codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers of AI systems, or by organisations representing them, or by both, including with the involvement of any interested stakeholders and their representative organisations such as civil society organisations and academia. Article 95(4) requires the AI Office and the Member States to take into account the specific interests and needs of SMEs, including start-ups, when encouraging and facilitating this process.
criteria_text: Codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers of AI systems, by organisations representing them, or both
May involve interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, including civil society and academia
The AI Office and the Member States must encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states that codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers, by organisations representing them, or by both, which matches the substance of criterion 1.
The answer explicitly mentions involvement of interested stakeholders and their representative organisations such as civil society and academia, satisfying the substance of criterion 2.
The answer directly states that the AI Office and Member States shall encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct, fulfilling criterion 3.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and logical flow; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what minimum elements must a provider's quality management system (QMS) for high-risk AI systems include? List the required elements.
rows.answer: Article 17(1) requires the quality management system to include: a strategy for regulatory compliance, design and development verification techniques, development and quality-control and quality-assurance techniques, examination, test and validation procedures, technical specifications including standards applied, systems and procedures for data management, the risk management system referred to in Article 9, the setting-up, implementation and maintenance of a post-market monitoring system under Article 72, procedures for serious incident reporting under Article 73, handling of communication with national competent authorities and other relevant bodies, systems and procedures for record-keeping, resource management including security-of-supply measures, and an accountability framework setting out management and staff responsibilities. Article 17(2) requires implementation to be proportionate to the provider's organisation size while ensuring the level of protection needed for compliance.
criteria_text: Regulatory compliance strategy incl. conformity assessment and modification management
Design, development, quality control and verification techniques/procedures
Examination, test and validation procedures and their frequency
Data management procedures across data lifecycle
Article 9 risk management system and Article 72 post-market monitoring system
Record-keeping and accountability framework for management/staff
criterion_remarks: The answer states the requirement for a strategy for regulatory compliance, including conformity assessment and modification management.
The answer includes design and development verification techniques, as well as development, quality control, and quality assurance techniques.
The answer explicitly mentions examination, test, and validation procedures, which covers the required element.
The answer refers to systems and procedures for data management, covering the data lifecycle aspect.
The answer includes both the risk management system under Article 9 and the post-market monitoring system under Article 72.
The answer includes systems and procedures for record-keeping and an accountability framework for management and staff.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured prose without self-reference or hedging, suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, in which specific situations may law enforcement use 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes (i.e., the exceptions to the prohibition)? List the permitted objectives.
rows.answer: Article 5(1)(h) prohibits real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement unless strictly necessary for one of three exhaustive objectives: (i) the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation, and for missing persons; (ii) the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety, or of a genuine and present or foreseeable terrorist attack; (iii) the localisation or identification of a suspect of a criminal offence listed in Annex II (which enumerates offences such as terrorism, murder, trafficking, and sexual exploitation of children) punishable by at least four years' custody. Each permitted use must also satisfy the procedural safeguards in Article 5(2), including a completed fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27 and registration in the EU database under Article 49.
criteria_text: Targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation, or missing persons
Prevention of specific, substantial and imminent threat to life/physical safety, or genuine terrorist attack threat
Localisation/identification of a suspect for investigation, prosecution, or executing a penalty for an Annex II offence punishable by at least 4 years custodial sentence/detention order
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states the targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation, and missing persons as a permitted objective.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must providers of AI systems that generate or manipulate synthetic content do to enable identification of AI-generated/manipulated output, and what quality criteria must that solution meet?
rows.answer: Article 50(2) requires providers of AI systems generating synthetic audio, image, video, or text content to ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. The technical solutions implementing this marking must be effective, interoperable, robust, and reliable as far as technically feasible, taking into account the specificities and limitations of various content types, the costs of implementation, and the generally acknowledged state of the art as may be reflected in relevant technical standards. This obligation does not apply where the system performs only an assistive function for standard editing, does not substantially alter the deployer's input data or its semantics, or where authorised by law for criminal-offence detection, prevention, investigation, or prosecution.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, which body has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models (Chapter V), and which entity is entrusted with implementing those tasks?
rows.answer: The Commission holds exclusive powers to supervise and enforce the Chapter V obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models under Article 88(1). The Commission entrusts the implementation of these tasks to the AI Office, without prejudice to the institutional powers set out in the Treaties. Article 88(2) adds a cooperation mechanism: national market surveillance authorities may request the Commission to exercise those enforcement powers where necessary and proportionate to assist their own tasks under the Regulation.

AI Office is entrusted with implementing these tasks

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what conditions must be met before data collected and processed for testing high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions can be transferred to a third country (outside the EU)?
rows.answer: Article 60(4)(e) governs this transfer: data collected and processed for real-world testing of high-risk AI systems may be transferred to a third country only where appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law are implemented. The provision does not define those safeguards autonomously but incorporates the existing Union data-transfer framework, principally the GDPR Chapter V mechanisms (adequacy decisions, standard contractual clauses, binding corporate rules, and the like). No additional AI Act-specific transfer condition applies beyond this requirement, so the provider or prospective provider must ensure that a recognised Union-law safeguard is in place before any such transfer occurs.
criteria_text: Appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law must be implemented for the transfer
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states that appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law must be implemented, which matches the substance of the criterion, and further explains that these safeguards are drawn from existing Union law frameworks like GDPR Chapter V.

rows.question: What are the conditions to classify general-purpose AI (GPAI) model as "GPAI model with systemic risk"? Do all need to be met at the same time?
rows.answer: No, not all conditions need to be met simultaneously. Under Article 51(1), a general-purpose AI model is classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk if it meets any of two alternative conditions: (a) it has high-impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools, methodologies, indicators and benchmarks, or (b) the Commission designates it, ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel, as having equivalent capabilities or impact, having regard to the Annex XIII criteria (number of parameters, dataset quality and size, training compute, input and output modalities, benchmarks, and reach). Article 51(2) creates a rebuttable presumption that condition (a) is met when cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating point operations.
criteria_text: Condition (a): high impact capabilities per Article 51(1)(a), presumed when training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs
Condition (b): Commission decision (ex officio or following qualified alert from scientific panel) that capabilities/impact are equivalent, per Annex XIII criteria
No, not cumulative - either condition alone suffices
criterion_remarks: The answer states the substance of condition (a) and explicitly identifies the 10^25 FLOPs threshold as a rebuttable presumption for high-impact capabilities, satisfying the criterion.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, is an AI system that is a safety component of a medical device classified as MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) automatically a high-risk AI system? Explain your reasoning.
rows.answer: No. Under Article 6(1), an AI system that is a safety component of a medical device listed in Annex I (point 11, Regulation (EU) 2017/745) is high-risk only where both conditions are met: the system is a safety component of a product covered by Annex I harmonisation legislation (Article 6(1)(a)), AND that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation (Article 6(1)(b)). MDR Class I devices (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) self-certify without a notified body, so the second condition is not fulfilled and the AI system is not automatically classified as high-risk under the EU AI Act.

Article 6(1)(a) and (b) are cumulative conditions
MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) devices undergo manufacturer self-assessment, not third-party conformity assessment
Condition (b) fails, so Article 6(1) does not apply

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, can an AI system intended to be used as a safety component in a lift qualify as a high-risk AI system, and under what conditions?
rows.answer: Yes. An AI system intended as a safety component in a lift can qualify as high-risk under Article 6(1), provided both cumulative conditions are met: first, under Article 6(1)(a), the system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and Annex I(4) expressly lists Directive 2014/33/EU on lifts and safety components for lifts; second, under Article 6(1)(b), the lift whose safety component is the AI system must be required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that Directive. Where both conditions hold, the provider must follow the relevant sectoral conformity assessment procedure under Article 43(3), which integrates the Chapter III Section 2 requirements into the Directive 2014/33/EU assessment.

Condition: that product (or the AI system itself as a product) required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation
Both conditions cumulative

rows.question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EU AI Act), how is "risk" defined?
rows.answer: ‘risk’ means the combination of the probability of an occurrence of harm and the severity of that harm;
criteria_text: Combination of probability of occurrence of harm and severity of that harm

rows.question: A provider becomes aware of a risk (within the meaning of Article 79(1)) for their high-risk AI system. Does the provider need to take immediate corrective action OR immediately investigate the causes OR both? For example, perhaps it's the market surveillance authority that must investigate the cause, and the provider can help later.
rows.answer: Article 20 imposes two concurrent immediate duties on the provider. Under Article 20(1), a provider that considers or has reason to consider its high-risk AI system is not in conformity must immediately take the necessary corrective actions (bringing the system into conformity, withdrawing, disabling, or recalling it) and inform distributors, deployers, authorised representatives, and importers. Under Article 20(2), where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) and the provider becomes aware of that risk, the provider must itself immediately investigate the causes, in collaboration with the reporting deployer where applicable, and inform the competent market surveillance authorities and, where relevant, the notified body of the nature of the non-compliance and any corrective action taken. The market surveillance authority has its own separate evaluation power under Article 79(2), but that authority-side procedure does not relieve the provider of its independent obligation to investigate and to act correctively at the same time.
criteria_text: Both
Immediate corrective action required under Article 20(1) where system is non-compliant
Immediate investigation of causes is the provider's own duty under Article 20(2)
Investigation done in collaboration with reporting deployer where applicable, not deferred to market surveillance authority

rows.question: My local small language model says that, as a distributor of high-risk AI systems, I must be careful that transport conditions do not jeopardize compliance. But AI is just software, isn't it? So I am pretty sure my model hallucinated. What do you say?
rows.answer: No, the local model did not hallucinate. Article 24(3) expressly requires distributors to ensure that, while a high-risk AI system is under their responsibility, storage or transport conditions, where applicable, do not jeopardise compliance with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements. The qualifier "where applicable" acknowledges that transport conditions may be irrelevant for purely software-based systems, but the obligation exists in the statute and applies whenever physical media, pre-configured hardware, or environmental conditions could affect system integrity.

rows.question: Does the AI Act prohibit or classifies as high-risk the use of AI in drones? Can I use AI in a drone to find who's around in town? And what if it's just a toy drone? And what about toy drones used for other applications?
rows.answer: The EU AI Act does not contain a blanket prohibition or a blanket high-risk classification for AI in drones. The classification depends on the drone's function and regulatory context across several provisions. Using an AI drone to identify "who's around in town" constitutes real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces. If operated by or on behalf of law enforcement, this is prohibited under Article 5(1)(h), subject only to the three narrow exceptions (victim search, imminent terrorist threat, serious-crime suspect localisation). Outside law enforcement, such biometric identification is high-risk under Annex III(1)(a), classified via Article 6(2). A toy drone with AI is a product covered by Directive 2009/48/EC (Annex I, point 2, toy safety). Where that toy requires third-party conformity assessment under the Toy Safety Directive, its AI component is high-risk under Article 6(1). A toy drone used for other applications beyond its intended toy purpose may additionally trigger Annex III use cases or, if repurposed as a safety component of machinery (Annex I, point 1), the Article 6(1) product-safety route.
criteria_text: No blanket prohibition/high-risk classification for drones as such — turns on AI system's intended use under Article 6
Drone AI identifying people in public = remote biometric identification, high-risk under Annex III(1)(a), not the 1:1 verification exclusion
Toy status irrelevant — classification depends on intended use, not the device
Toy drone used for other application is high-risk only if that use matches Annex III (or Article 6(1) safety-component/conformity-assessment criteria)

The answer clarifies that a toy drone used for other applications is high-risk only if the use falls under Annex III or meets the Article 6(1) safety-component and conformity-assessment criteria.

rows.question: We deployed a high-risk AI system in our company. We have a use in mind that is outside the intended use and our legal team say such a use is definitely no risk (no Annex I nor III apply). Can we just go ahead with the new use and do we need to keep logs for it?
rows.answer: No, the deployer cannot simply proceed. Modifying the intended purpose of a high-risk AI system so that it is used outside its designated purpose triggers Article 25(1)(c), which reclassifies the deployer as a provider and imposes all provider obligations, including a new conformity assessment under Article 43, regardless of the legal team's view that neither Annex I nor Annex III applies. The log-retention duty under Article 26(6) requires deployers of high-risk AI systems to keep automatically generated logs for at least six months, but that obligation is tied to the system's intended purpose as a high-risk system, not to a new, unclassified use. Before any repurposing, the deployer-turned-provider must cooperate with the original provider under Article 25(2) and complete the documentation and conformity steps required for the modified intended purpose.

Article 26(1) requires use in accordance with instructions for use; deviating from intended use is not excused merely because that use alone wouldn't trigger Annex III
Yes, logging duty under Article 26(6) still applies regardless of the particular use

rows.question: Is AI software that helps clinicians take medical decisions around best treatment potentially high-risk? According to what Article and/or Annex?
rows.answer: Yes, AI software that helps clinicians decide on best treatment is potentially high-risk through two routes. First, under Article 6(1) read with Annex I (item 11, the Medical Device Regulation 2017/745), clinical-decision software qualifying as a medical device that requires third-party conformity assessment (typically Class IIa, IIb, or III under MDR Annex VIII) is high-risk. Second, under Article 6(2) read with Annex III(5)(a), an AI system used to evaluate eligibility for healthcare services by or on behalf of a public authority is independently high-risk, and under Annex III(5)(c) if it performs risk assessment and pricing for life or health insurance.

Article 6(2)
Annex III (healthcare access/provision)

rows.question: About obligations of transparency to providers who want to use a GPAI model, do you need to disclose: date of release? number of paramaters? applicable model interaction with hardware? license? samples of outlier data used in training? Given clear yes/no to each item.
rows.answer: The governing provision is Article 53(1)(b), which requires GPAI providers to supply downstream AI system providers with the information set out in Annex XII. Taking each item against Annex XII's mandatory elements. Date of release: Yes, required under Annex XII(1)(c). Number of parameters: Yes, required under Annex XII(1)(f), which mandates disclosure of architecture and number of parameters. Model interaction with hardware: Yes, required under Annex XII(1)(d), covering how the model interacts with hardware or software not part of the model itself. Licence: Yes, required under Annex XII(1)(h). Samples of outlier data used in training: No. Annex XII(2)(c) requires information on training data including type, provenance, and curation methodologies, but neither Annex XII nor Annex XI requires disclosure of actual data samples, including outlier samples. Annex IV(2)(d), applicable to high-risk AI system technical documentation, references outlier detection as a data-cleaning methodology to be described, but this concerns methodology description, not sample disclosure.

Architecture and number of parameters - Yes
Interaction with hardware or software - Yes
License - Yes
Samples of outlier training data - No

rows.question: Name the areas of high-risk use cases. Is healthcare decision making one of them?
rows.answer: Annex III lists eight areas of high-risk use cases under Article 6(2): biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, access to and enjoyment of essential private and public services and benefits, law enforcement, migration and asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes. Yes, healthcare decision making falls within this framework through multiple routes: Annex III(5)(a) covers AI evaluating eligibility for essential public services including healthcare, Annex III(5)(c) covers life and health insurance risk assessment, Annex III(5)(d) covers emergency healthcare patient triage, and Article 6(1) with Annex I captures AI that is a safety component of a medical device requiring third-party conformity assessment.
criteria_text: Biometrics; Critical infrastructure; Education and vocational training; Employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; Access to and enjoyment of essential private and public services and benefits; Law enforcement; Migration, asylum and border control management; Administration of justice and democratic processes
No

rows.question: Could the introduction of guardrails in an AI agentic system reduce the risk of the system from high risk to moderate risk? What about changing the capabilities and intended use of the system?
rows.answer: No. The EU AI Act does not recognise a "moderate risk" tier, so no technical measure can move a system from high-risk to that category. High-risk classification under Article 6 is binary: a system is high-risk if it is a safety component of an Annex I product requiring third-party conformity assessment (Article 6(1)) or falls within an Annex III use case (Article 6(2)). Adding guardrails does not change the classification; it instead satisfies the Article 9 risk management obligation, which requires targeted risk-control measures proportionate to the identified risks. The Article 6(3) derogation can remove an Annex III system from high-risk status, but only where it performs a narrow procedural task, improves a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns without replacing human assessment, or performs a preparatory task, and never where it profiles natural persons. Changing the intended purpose so the system no longer falls within an Annex III use case or no longer serves as a safety component under Annex I would remove the high-risk classification entirely, but under Article 25(1)(c) the party making that modification assumes provider obligations if the change makes a non-high-risk system high-risk.
criteria_text: No - guardrails alone do not create an intermediate "moderate risk" tier; the Act's Article 6(3) derogation is binary (high-risk or exempted)

Exemption applies only where the system's intended task itself meets one of four Article 6(3) conditions: narrow procedural task; improving a previously completed human activity; detecting deviations from prior decisions without replacing human assessment; or a preparatory task
Yes - changing the system's capabilities/intended use can exit high-risk status if the redefined task now satisfies one of those conditions
Exception: an AI system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk, regardless of guardrails or intended-use changes

rows.question: Is the use of deep-fake images in university classes to represent e.g. skin conditions in patients allowed? Does the artificial nature of the content need to be disclosed for such an evidently educational and illustrative use? If so, does the lighter transparency requirement apply like for certain law enforcement situations?
rows.answer: Yes, the use is allowed, but the artificial nature must still be disclosed. Article 50(4) requires deployers of deep fake content to disclose that it has been artificially generated or manipulated, and this obligation applies even in educational settings. However, where the content forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional, or analogous work or programme, Article 50(4) limits the transparency duty to disclosing the existence of such content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work. The law-enforcement exemption in Article 50(4), which disapplies the obligation entirely where use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate, or prosecute criminal offences, does not apply to educational illustration; the lighter regime that applies here is the "evidently creative or analogous work" accommodation, not the law-enforcement carve-out.
criteria_text: Yes, permitted
Disclosure still required under Article 50(4)
Lighter regime applies as "analogous work" to artistic/creative/fictional content — only existence of generated content must be disclosed, without hampering display/enjoyment
Law-enforcement carve-out is a full exemption, not a lighter regime, and is inapplicable here
criterion_remarks: The answer states that the use is allowed, which matches the 'Yes, permitted' criterion.
The answer explicitly states that disclosure is required under Article 50(4), satisfying the criterion.
The answer identifies that the lighter transparency requirement applies via the 'analogous work' category, aligning with the criterion.
The answer correctly distinguishes the law-enforcement carve-out as a full exemption inapplicable here, noting it does not apply to educational use.

rows.question: A supermarket uses an AI tool that analyzes only current-cart and checkout anomalies (no biometrics, no face recognition, no sensitive-trait inference, no cross-context social scoring) to flag transactions for optional manual bag checks by store staff. The retailer claims this is "high risk like policing", as it: resembles investigation of potentially criminal offences (theft) + evaluates or classifies persons based on observed behaviour in a way that may lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment. Is this situation potentially high-risk?
rows.answer: Not high-risk. The system described is not operated by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, so it falls outside Annex III(6), which covers AI used for law enforcement purposes such as individual criminal risk assessment or investigation of offences. Article 5(1)(d) prohibits AI that assesses the risk of a natural person committing a criminal offence based solely on profiling or personality traits, but a cart-anomaly detector flags transactional irregularities from objective, verifiable checkout data, not personality-based crime prediction. Article 5(1)(c) prohibits social scoring, yet this system analyses single-transaction anomalies within the same retail context rather than evaluating persons over time based on social behaviour across multiple contexts with a score leading to unrelated or disproportionate treatment. A private retailer's checkout-anomaly tool that triggers only an optional manual bag check, uses no biometrics, and does not profile personality traits is neither prohibited nor high-risk under the Act. It is a minimal-risk system with no mandatory obligations beyond the horizontal AI literacy duty under Article 4.
criteria_text: No
Annex III.6 categories apply only where the AI system is used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities (or by Union institutions/bodies in support of law enforcement authorities)

A supermarket's own loss-prevention/bag-check tool, run by store staff, is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, so it falls outside Annex III.6 regardless of its resemblance to investigative or evaluative functions

rows.question: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?
rows.answer: No. The Chapter III Section 2 requirements (Articles 9 to 15) cannot be skipped. Article 43(3) expressly states that where a Section A Annex I legal act allows the manufacturer to opt out of third-party conformity assessment by applying all harmonised standards, the manufacturer may use that option only if it has also applied harmonised standards or common specifications covering all requirements set out in Section 2 of Chapter III. The system remains high-risk under Article 6(1) because it is a safety component of an Annex I product, and the substantive obligations of Section 2 apply in full; the opt-out merely changes the assessment procedure, not the underlying requirements.

Section 2 requirements still apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment (Art. 43(3), second sentence)
The third-party opt-out under sectoral legislation is available only if harmonised standards/common specifications applied cover ALL Section 2 requirements, not just the sectoral ones
